title: Gene Editing and Precision Medicine: India's Biotech Opportunity and Genetic-Data Challenge
fullText:
CURRENT AFFAIRS 208
Gene Editing and Precision Medicine: India's Biotech Opportunity
and Genetic-Data Challenge
Category
GS
Date
Quick rule
Science & Technology / Health
GS III / GS II
12 Sep 2026
Read highlighted facts first
FAST READ - read only this box if short on time
• Biotech Conclave 2026 highlighted gene editing, precision medicine, indigenous biopharma capability and protection
of genetic data.
• India already has regulatory guidance for gene-therapy product development and clinical trials involving bodies such
as CDSCO, ICMR and DBT.
• The policy challenge is to combine affordable innovation with biosafety, ethics, informed consent and genomic-data
protection.
WHY IN NEWS
• Rapid advances in CRISPR, cell and gene therapies are moving biotechnology from broad population treatment
toward more personalised interventions.
• India's scale, disease burden and research capacity create opportunity, but genetic data is uniquely sensitive because
it is persistent and partly shared with biological relatives.
TOP DATA & FACTS
• Gene editing deliberately alters genetic material at targeted locations.
• CRISPR systems are widely used research tools for targeted editing.
• Precision medicine tailors prevention or treatment using individual biological characteristics.
• Gene therapy may add, silence, replace or edit genetic material.
• India has National Guidelines for Gene Therapy Product Development and Clinical Trials, 2019.
• CDSCO is India's central drug regulator.
• ICMR develops biomedical research and ethical guidance.
• DBT supports biotechnology research and policy.
• India has supported clinical research in gene therapy, including haemophilia.
• Genetic data can reveal disease predisposition and ancestry information.
• Genomic information can have implications for biological relatives, not only the sampled individual.
• Informed consent must address future use, storage and sharing of samples and data.
• Re-identification risk can persist even after simple removal of names.
• Equitable access is important because advanced therapies can be extremely expensive.
• One Health links human, animal and environmental health.

PRELIMS
• CRISPR is a gene-editing technology, not a vaccine platform by definition.
• Precision medicine is broader than gene editing.
• CDSCO regulates drugs; ICMR is a research/ethics institution; DBT promotes biotechnology.
• Somatic editing affects treated body cells; germline editing raises heritable-change concerns.
• Genetic data can remain sensitive over long periods.
• Clinical translation requires both scientific evidence and regulatory oversight.
QUICK REVISION
Build answers around four pillars: innovation, safety, ethics and access. Add CDSCO-ICMR-DBT, 2019 gene-therapy
guidelines, consent, genetic-data protection, affordability and indigenous biomanufacturing.
PROBABLE OBJECTIVE QUESTION
With reference to the above topic, consider the following statements:
1. Precision medicine may use genetic and other biological information to tailor care.
2. India has national guidance for gene-therapy product development and clinical trials.
3. All gene editing necessarily produces heritable changes in future generations.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
(a) 1 and 3 only
(b) 2 and 3 only
(c) 1 and 2 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3
Answer: (c) 1 and 2 only
Explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Somatic gene editing need not be heritable; germline editing raises distinct
heritability concerns.

PROBABLE MAINS QUESTION
India's biotechnology ambitions must advance together with genomic-data governance and bioethics. Discuss with
reference to gene editing and precision medicine.
MODEL ANSWER - ~300 WORDS
INTRODUCTION
Rapid advances in CRISPR, cell and gene therapies are moving biotechnology from broad population treatment toward
more personalised interventions. The policy challenge is to combine affordable innovation with biosafety, ethics,
informed consent and genomic-data protection.
SIGNIFICANCE
• Indigenous biotechnology can reduce import dependence and address diseases important to the Global South.
• Precision medicine can improve targeting and reduce ineffective treatment.
• Biomanufacturing can create high-value research and industrial capacity.
CHALLENGES
• Safety risks include off-target effects and uncertain long-term outcomes.
• Genetic privacy, consent and discrimination concerns are unusually persistent.
• High treatment costs can widen health inequality.
WAY FORWARD
• Strengthen interoperable regulation across research, drugs, ethics and data protection.
• Require long-term follow-up, transparent consent and secure genomic-data governance.
• Support public research, local manufacturing and access models for high-cost therapies.
Regulation must also distinguish somatic interventions, which affect treated individuals, from heritable germline changes that raise deeper intergenerational concerns. Standards for laboratory validation, clinical evidence, long-term surveillance and adverse-event reporting should evolve with the technology. Cross-border transfer of genomic datasets requires equally careful governance because privacy harm can persist long after a research project ends.

CONCLUSION
Biotechnology leadership will be durable only if scientific capability is matched by public trust, ethical safeguards and
affordable access.
India also needs governance for the full genomic-data life cycle: collection, sequencing, storage, research access,
secondary use and eventual deletion or archival. Consent should be specific enough to be meaningful while allowing
ethically approved research. Security standards must recognise that a genome cannot simply be reset like a password
after a breach. Publicly supported biobanks and clinical programmes should use independent ethics review and
benefit-sharing principles. At the same time, local manufacturing and clinical-trial capacity can reduce cost so advanced
therapies do not remain limited to a small affluent population.
